The legates from that same council of Rome, who had anathematized him, themselves served to break the eightied ecumenical council. How much has changed among men! How much what was false becomes true according to the times! The legates of Jean VIII wrote in full council; if anyone does not recognize Photius, whose sharing is with Judas, the council writes for many years on patriarch Photius and on patriarch Jean. Finally, after the acts of the council, one sees a letter from the Pope to this learned patriarch, in which he says: we think as you do... etc., it is therefore clear that the Roman church and the Greek church thought differently than what is thought today. It happened since Rome adopted the procession of the father and son; and it even happened that in 1274, the emperor of the Greeks, Michael Palaeologus, imploring against the Turks a new crusade, sent to the second council of Lyon his patriarch and his chancellor, who sang with the council in Latin, which ex patre filioque procedit. But the Greek church returned even more to its opinion, and seemed to leave it even more in the passing meeting that took place with Eugene IV. May men learn from there how to tolerate each other. The government of Hussein was despised, and the province of Candahar having begun the troubles, the provinces of Caucasia on the side of Georgia also revolted. Finally, Maghmud besieged Isfahan in 1722. Hussein handed this capital over to him, abdicated the kingdom at his feet, and recognized him for his master; too happy that Maghmud dared to marry his daughter. All the scenes of cruelty and misfortune that we examine from the times of Charlemagne have nothing more horrible than the aftermath of the Isfahan revolution. Maghmud believed he could only consolidate himself by murdering the families of the principal citizens. The entire Persia had been thirty years as much as Germany was before the Peace of Westphalia; what was France under Charles VI, and what was England in the Wars of the Roses red and white? But Persia fell from a state more flourishing into one greater abyss of misfortunes. Religion too increased at these desolations. The Agha held for Omar as Persians hold for Ali; and this Maghmud chief of the Aghas mixed the most lax superstitions with the most detestable cruelties. He died in madness in 1725 after having desolated Persia. A new usurper of the nation of the Agha succeeded him; he was called Asraf. The desolation of Persia doubled on all sides. The Turks flooded it from the side of Georgia, the ancient Colchis.

They took Nicomedia, they struck twice on the armies commanded by Soliman's son. The Turks and Arabs could not withstand in these beginnings the shock of these multitudes covered with iron, and of their great battle horses, and of the forests of lances into which they were not accustomed. Albert Durer, born in Nuremberg in 1470, whose name I have spoken as a painter when referring to his school, leaves little to desire in his works, including those of his contemporaries, who themselves would benefit if this distinguished artist had known antiquity, so that his figures could possess both elegance and truth. Aldegraf (Albert), born in Westphalia, a disciple of Durer, has grasped his manner, and once gained great renown. Audran (Gérard), died in 1703 at the age of sixty-three, practiced his brush to multiply large pieces from Poussin, Mignard, and others. His magnificent prints of Alexander's battles, which he engraved after the designs of Le Brun, are well known; the work of this artist is recommended by force and good taste in its manner. Baldini (Baccio), a Florentine, was an apprentice to Maso Finiguerra, inventor of the secret of copper printing, and flourished even more than his master. Belle (Etienne de la), born in Florence in 1610 and died in the same city in 1664, acquired a method of watercolor that is very rapid and has such a strong effect that a few curious people put it above Callot's. If this master's method is not so refined in engraving nor so precise in design as Callot's, his touch is more free, more sophisticated, and more picturesque; few have surpassed him in spirit, finesse, and the playfulness of the point. He generally neglected the details and hands of his small figures, but his heads possess a nobility and a beautiful character that is seducing; his work is very considerable. Bénédette Castiglione, painter and engraver, born in Gènes in 1616 and died in Mantua in 1670, etched several pieces with watercolor where he infused as much spirit as taste. The dark tones of his prints are the charm of connoisseurs.

The successes of this conquering people seem to be due rather to the enthusiasm that animates them and to the spirit of the nation, which belongs to its conductors: for Omar was assassinated by a Persian slave in 653. Otman, his successor, took office in 655 during an uprising. Ali, this famous cousin of Muhammad, is not elected and governs only amidst turmoil. He dies assassinated after five years like his predecessors, and yet the Muslim arms are always happy. This Ali, which the Persians revered today and whom they follow whose principles stand in opposition to those of Omar, finally obtained the caliphate and transferred the seat of the caliphs from the city of Medina, where Muhammad is buried, into the city of Coufa on the banks of the Euphrates: barely remains - there are now ruins. This is the fate of Babylon, Seleucia, and all the ancient cities of Caldaea, which were built only of bricks. It is evident that the genius of the Arab people stirred by Muhammad put everything in motion itself—even for nearly three centuries, and resembling in this regard the genius of the ancient Romans. Indeed, under Valid, the least warlike of the caliphs, the greatest conquests are made. One of his generals extends his empire to Samarkand in 707. Another attacks the empire of the Greeks toward the Black Sea. Another in 711 passes from Egypt into the easily conquered Spain alternately subdued by the Carthaginians, the Romans, the Goths and Vandals, and finally by these Arabs whom they call Maurites. They established there the kingdom of Cordoba. The Sultan of Egypt truly shakes the yoke of the great caliph of Baghdad, and Abd al-Rahman, governor of conquered Spain, no longer recognizes the Sultan of Egypt: however everything is still under Muslim arms. This Abd al-Rahman, small son of the caliph Hisham, takes over the kingdoms of Castile, Navarre, Portugal, Aragon.

Finally, Roland or Raoul, the most illustrious of these northern brigands, after having been expelled from Dannemarck, having gathered in Scandinavia all those who wished to attach themselves to his fortune, attempted new ventures and laid the foundation for the hope of his greatness on Europe's weakness. He approached England, where his compatriots were already established; but after two useless victories, he turned towards France, which other Normans knew how to ruin, but whom they could not subjugate. Roland was the only among these barbarians who ceased to deserve his name by seeking a fixed settlement. Master of Rouen without difficulty, instead of destroying it, he raised its walls and towers. Rouen became his place of arms; from there he raided both England and France, waging war with political skill as well as with fury. France was crumbling under the reign of Charles the Simple, king by name, and whose monarchy was becoming even more fragmented by dukes, counts, and barons than by Normans. Charles the Gros had given only gold to the barbarians; Charles the Simple offered Roland his daughter and provinces. Raoul asked to settle in Normandy: and they were too happy to give it to him. He then requested Brittany; there was dispute; but he had to cede it again, with clauses that the strongest always exploited to his advantage. Thus Brittany, which at that time was all - to - the hour a kingdom, became a fief of the Neustrie; and the Neustrie, which soon learned to name Normandy after its usurpers, was an independent state, whose dukes paid a vain homage to the crown of France. The archbishop of Rouen convinced Roland to become a Catholic. This prince willingly embraced a religion that affirmed his power. The true conquerors are those who know how to make laws. Their power is stable; others are temporary structures that pass. Peaceful Roland was the only legislator among his contemporaries in the Christian continent.

We had already elected King of Romans in Germany, Conrad son of Frederick II, but it was necessary, to please the Pope, to choose another Emperor. This new Caesar was neither chosen by the Dukes of Saxony or Brabant or Bavaria or Austria nor by any prince of the empire. The archbishops of Strasbourg, Würzburg, Spire, Metz, with those of Mainz, Cologne and Trèves, created this Emperor. They chose a Landgrave of Thuringia, whom they appealed to as King of Priests. From the Strait to which this navigator gave his name, he sailed west-north-west until reaching the equator, passing at 9858 miles from the strait, and towards the 170th degree of eastern longitude of Paris; and in this long passage, he discovered only two small uninhabited islands, separated from each other by two hundred leagues. Knowing: Saint Peter, at 18 or 19 degrees south latitude; the Island of the Typhoons, at 14 or 15 degrees south latitude; and the Island of St. Vincent, at 14 degrees 15 minutes south latitude. These islands, which Magellan named generally as the Islands of Misfortune, are still unknown, and they were not marked on the map of the equatorial great ocean because their position is not indicated in a sufficiently precise manner. Of all the islands discovered since Magellan, it is only the Island of Savage by Cook and the Lost Child by Bougainville that can represent the two Islands of Misfortune: they are two hundred leagues apart from each other, as they are from one another, and roughly by their latitude; the Savage, at 19 degrees 1 minute south latitude, and 172 degrees 30 minutes west longitude of Paris; the Lost Child, at 14 degrees 6 minutes south latitude, and 179 degrees 2 minutes east longitude.

It thus descended from the Alps with an army; and Rome was stained with blood for this dispute over the cross and the ring. Treaties, perjuries, excommunications, and murders followed one after another with rapidity. Pope II had regularly annulled his oath with a sworn promise on the Gospel, yet he annulled his own oath by cardinals; a new way of failing to keep his word. He was treated as a liar and a prevaricator even in the council, so that he was compelled to reclaim what he had given. Then another intrusion of the emperor into Rome; for almost never did these emperors enter there except for ecclesiastical quarrels, the greatest being the crowning. Finally, after having created, deposed, expelled, and repelled the popes as often as his father, Henry V was also excommunicated as frequently as his father, and equally troubled by his own great vassals in Germany; he was thus compelled to finish the struggle over investiture, renouncing this cross and ring. He did more; he resigned himself regularly to the right that emperors were granted to appoint bishops, or to interpose their authority in elections so that they were absolutely masters of them. It was therefore decided at a council held in Rome that kings would no longer give the investitures canonically elected by a staff, but by a rod.

In 1255, Pope Alexander III established the inquisition in France under King Louis. The guard of the Cordeliers of Paris and the provincial of the Dominicans were the great inquisitors. They were required, by Alexander's bull, to consult the bishops, but they did not depend on them. This strange jurisdiction given to men who make vows of renunciation was disgraceful to both clergy and laity. A cordelier inquisitor attended the trial of the Templars; but soon, the uprising of all minds left these monks with only an useless title. In Italy, the popes had more credibility because any disobedience they showed was greater than they were in Rome, farther away than they ever were, they remained always at the head of the Guelph faction, against the Gelosi. They used this inquisition against supporters of the empire. Because in 1302 Pope John XXII carried out proceedings by inquisitors' monks against Matthew Visconti, lord of Milan, whose crime was to be attached to Emperor Louis de Boièvre. The loyalty of the vassal to his suzerain was declared heresy; the Malatesta family were treated alike for the same reason; and if the successor did not follow the sentence, it was that he was then easier for the popes to have inquisitors than armies. The more this tribunal established itself, and the more bishops who were thought to be theirs were denied a right that seemed theirs, they demanded it vigorously. The popes associated them with the inquisitorial monks, who exercised their authority fully in almost all states of Italy, and whose bishops were merely assessors. Toward the end of the thirteenth century, in 1289, Venice had already received the inquisition; but elsewhere it was entirely dependent on the pope, it was under Venetian control, subject to the Senate. The wisest precaution taken was that the fines and confiscations did not belong to the inquisitors.

After the reports of M De Vaujuas and M Boutin, it was evident that we could not find at the Trinity the water and wood that we were lacking. I decided immediately to take a route for the Sainte-Catherine Island on the coast of Brazil: this was the former release point of French ships heading into the South Sea. Frézier and Admiral Anson found abundantly enough to supply all their needs there. To not lose even one day, I gave preference to the Sainte-Catherine Island over Rio-Janéiro, where the various formalities would have required more time than it was necessary to obtain the water and wood we were lacking. But by directing my route toward the Sainte-Catherine Island, I wished to ensure the existence of the Ascención Island, which M De Vaujuas placed at a hundred leagues west of the Trinity, and only 15 minutes further south. Following the journal of M Poncel de La Haye, who commanded the renowned frigate, I was certain that different navigators, including Frézier, a very enlightened man, had come to Ascención, and that they had been truly at the Trinity only. Despite the authority of M Poncel de La Haye, I thought this geographical point deserved further clarification. The two days we spent heading southward the part of the island of the Trinity put us within reach of making the relays after which M Bernizet drew up the plan for the southern part of the island: it differs very little from that of Dr. Halley, who had been entrusted to me by M De Fleurieu. The view painted by M Duché de Vancy is so striking a truth that alone will suffice for navigators coming into the southern part of the Trinity never to be able to make any mistake.

text: Ignoring the era of their division into Ostrogoths and Visigoths, it is only mentioned that this division was already established from the time of Emperor Claudius II. Perhaps the Danube was the occasion for naming the Ostrogoths or Eastern Goths, those who remained on the left bank of this river, and the Visigoths or Western Goths, those who settled beyond it and on the right. Always is certain that the Goths became two distinct nations who took different paths and had very different destinies; and this distinction between the two Gothic nations was most clearly defined under Emperor Valens around the year 370. They then submitted to two kings: Fritigerus governed the Visigoths, and Othonaric the Ostrogoths. These latter attached themselves to the Eastern Empire and adopted Arianism that they carried in Italy, Gauls, and Spain. Both victors and vanquished, they finally obtained Thrace and were sufficiently tranquil as long as Emperor Theodosius reigned; but after his death they attacked the Roman Empire under Radagalys, and then under Alaric who took Rome, the pillage, and ended his days in Cyzicus. Ataulphemus, his successor, fell in love with the sister of Emperor Honorius, married her, ceded the empire to his eunuch, and retreated into Gaul with a part of his Visigoths; the other part preferred to remain in Italy where it became so powerful that Odoacer found the secret of usurping the throne and seizing sovereign authority. Theodoric departed from Thrace with his Ostrogoths, defeated Odoacer, and began the kingdom of the Ostrogoths in Italy; I say kingdom, because this prince contented himself with the title of king and made his residence in Ravenna. His successors quarreled with Emperor Justinian, who destroyed their monarchy by the victories of Belisarius and Narses; since that time, which is from the year 552, there is no longer any mention of the Ostrogoths in history. About six years after Alboin came to Italy and founded the kingdom of the Lombards.

CHAPTER 97 General Idea of the Seventeenth Century. The beginning of the seventeenth century that we have already begun presents both the greatest spectacles that the world has ever known. If one casts the net over those who ruled for their time in Europe, their glory, or their conduct, or the great changes they were the cause of, render their names immortal. It is to Constantinople a Selim who puts under Ottoman domination Syria and Egypt, whose Mamluks had been in possession since the thirteenth century. Then comes his son, the great Soliman, who first among the Turkish emperors marches to Vienna, and is crowned king of Persia in Baghdad seized by his arms, making Europe and Asia tremble alike. On the same terms, towards the north, Gustav Vasa breaks the yoke of foreign rule in Sweden, elected king of the country, whom he is the liberator. In Moscow, Jean Basilowitz liberates his homeland from the Tartars to whom it was tributary; a prince truly barbaric, and leader of an even more barbarous nation; but the avenger of his country deserves to be counted among the great princes.

Until then, the gross manners of this court had not yet adopted the policy of the sultans, and former Greek emperors, of sacrificing princes of blood to ensure the safety of the throne. A first minister named Boris-Gudenou, whose father-in-law Fedor had married his sister, persuaded the czar Fedor that only by imitating the Turks could one rule well, and that he should kill his brother. This first minister, Boris, sent an officer into the village where young Demetri was raised, with orders to kill him. The officer who returned said he had carried out his commission and asked for the reward promised to him. Boris, for any reward, killed the murderer in order to erase the evidence of the crime. It is said that Boris, some time after poisoning the czar Fedor; and though he was suspected, he did not rise to the throne nonetheless. Then it appeared in Lithuania a young man who claimed to be Prince Demetri, escaped from the assassin. Several people who had known him came forward and recognized him by certain marks on his mother's face. He resembled the prince perfectly; he wore the gold cross enriched with gems that were attached to the neck of Demetri at his baptism. A palatine of Sandomir recognized him as the son of Jean Basilide, and as the true czar.

He discovers: the island of Pâques, located at 27 degrees 4 minutes south latitude and 265 degrees 42 minutes east longitude from the meridian of Ténériffe, according to the author of the lives of the governors of Batavia; which corresponds to 113 degrees 18 minutes west of the meridian of Paris: inhabited island, covered with sixteen Dutch circles of latitude, and notable for colossal statues or figures erected in large numbers along its coasts; (it was recognized since by Cook, who found it at 27 degrees 5 minutes south latitude and 112 degrees 6 minutes east longitude west of Paris, and who named it Easter or Pâques): it was also seen in 1770 by the Spanish, who placed it by 27 degrees 6 minutes south latitude and 268 degrees 19 minutes east longitude west of Ténériffe, which corresponds to 110 degrees 41 minutes of our longitude, west of Paris; these latter gave it the name San Carlos.

Charls-Hof, or Charles's Court, at 15 degrees 45 minutes south latitude, and after eight hundred leagues of course from the island of Pâques: (according to French relations of this voyage, it is a small bare island with a kind of lake in its interior.) Roggewein believed that this was the island of the Dogs of Le Maire and Schouten, and the Dutch relation does not assign it either latitude or longitude: they placed it on the map relative to its distance from the islands of Pernicieux, which are twelve leagues west; whose position is now known.

The islands of Pernicieux, at 14 degrees 41 minutes south latitude and twelve Dutch circles to the west of Charls-Hof: these are four low-lying inhabited islands, which have been since four to ten leagues off; (Roggewein lost a vessel there, which gave the name Pernicieuse to one of these islands; two others were called the Two Brothers, and another the Mother; it remained five men from the crew, who deserted and were abandoned.)

The siege and defense of Leyden are among the greatest testimonies to what constancy and freedom can achieve. The Dutch did exactly the same thing that they were willing to risk in 1672 when Louis XIV was at the gates of Amsterdam; they breached the dikes; the waters of the Issel, Meuse, and the ocean flooded the countryside; and a fleet of two hundred ships brought aid into the city through the works of the Spanish. Another miracle occurred; it is that the besiegers dared to continue the siege and attempt to drain this vast flooding. There was no precedent in history for such a resourcefulness among besieged cities, nor such resoluteness among besieging forces; but this resoluteness proved futile, and Leyden celebrates today every year on the day of its liberation. It is not worth forgetting that the inhabitants used pigeons during this siege to send news to Prince William III: this is a common practice in Asia. What was this wise and boastful government of Philip II when one sees in these terms—even his troops mutinied in Flanders due to unpaid wages, sacked Antwerp, and all the provinces of the Netherlands, without consulting him or his governor, enter into a treaty of pacification with the rebels, publish an amnesty, release prisoners, demolish fortresses, and order that the famous statue of Duke Albe be torn down—the trophy that his pride had raised to its cruelty—and which was still standing in the citadel of Antwerp, whose master was the king? After the death of the great commander of Requesenens, Philip, who could no longer risk trying to restore peace in the Netherlands by his presence, sent Don Juan d'Autriche, his brother, as his cousin; prince renowned throughout Europe for the famous victory at Lepanto over the Turks and for his ambition which had led him to attempt to become king of Tunis. Philip did not like Don Juan; he feared his fame, and challenged his plans.

There was only the rear guard, composed of small vassals, who remained loyal and continued to serve at various times. It is surprising that after so many disasters France possessed such resources and money. But a rich country by its provisions never ceases to be when culture is not abandoned. Civil wars shake the body of the state and do not destroy it. Murders and lootings, which desolate families, enrich others. Negotiators become just as skilled as they need more art to save themselves amidst so many storms. Jacques Coeur is a great example of this. He had established the largest trade that no particular person in Europe had ever embraced. Since him only Cosme de Médicis has matched his achievement. Jacques Coeur had three hundred factors in Italy and the Levant. He lent two hundred thousand ducats to the king, without which one would never have regained Normandy. His industry was more useful during peace than during war, when Dunois and the Pucelle were not as helpful. This is a great blot on his memory that Charles VII persecuted such an individual as necessary. We know nothing about him, because who knows the secrets revealed by human faults and injustices? The king had him imprisoned, and the parliament tried him. Nothing could be proven against him except that he had made a Christian slave a chriutian slave, which had left and betrayed its master, and that he had sold arms to the Sudan of Egypt. On these two actions, one was permitted, and the other virtuous, he was condemned to lose his possessions. He found in his commissaries more justice than in the courtiers who lost theirs. They all contributed almost equally to help him in his disgrace. Jacques Coeur continued his trade in Cyprus and never had the courage to return to his ungrateful homeland, although he was expelled there.

It is true that these renoncers must have some legitimate cause, and that kings would inflict great hardship on their successors if they withdrew a province from the body of state without being constrained to do so, or without finding there great advantages. But when they consent to these withdrawals only by necessity, or for the good and utility of the kingdom, their successors have no subject to complain about them; and if they do, most of our kings would have had the right to complain about their predecessors, particularly the sons of Henry II, who by the treaty of Château de Cambrai released and returned nearly two cens cities or fortresses. It must be added to this that it is difficult to mark this point of greatness on which the author speaks, that in the states that have come, it is no longer permitted to kings withdraw any part; because it has never passed a considerable period since the establishment of monarchy that France has increased by the conquests of our kings, or diminished by those of our neighbors. Moreover, the kings of the first and second race have very often lost its greatness, sharing it between their sons, and dividing the kingdom into several kingdoms. Finally, to avoid aggravating all provinces united from the crown, it is enough to say that Burgundy was held by King Henry, little son of Hugh Capet, in favor of Robert his brother; that it returned under King Jean, who shortly after gave it to Philippe le Hardoy, fourth son; and that after the death of Charles the last Duke of Burgundy, Louis XI made him master; so that he had not fifty years when it was reclaimed from the crown when François I wished to cede it. Now let us pass on to other pretexts for which one takes leave to dispense with the fidelity owed to sovereigns.

What is more singular than this is that Urban II, who uttered this sentence, spoke it within the very courts of the king, in Clermont in Auvergne, where he came to seek an ale, and in the same council where we will see that he preached the crusade. However, it appears not at all that the excommunicated Philip was horrified by his subjects; this is another reason to doubt this general abandonment where it is said that King Robert had been reduced. What is quite remarkable is the marriage of King Henry Père of Philip with a princess from Moscow. The Moscovites, or Russians, were beginning to be Eastern Orthodox; but they had no trade with the rest of Europe. They lived beyond Poland, scarcely Eastern Orthodox herself, and without any correspondence with France. However, King Henry sent to Russia requesting the daughter of the sovereign, whom other Europeans granted the title of duke, also, well as at the head of Poland. The Russians called them in their language "tzaar," from which we have since taken the word "tsar." It is said that Henry determined himself to this marriage out of fear of stirring ecclesiastical quarrels. Of all the superstitions of these matters—not least the one of not being able to marry his parent at the seventh degree—this was by far the most harmful to the good of states; for it prevented him from marrying his cousin at the seventh degree. Almost all European sovereigns were by parens with Henry. Whatever the matter, Anna, daughter of Jaroslaw, Tsar of Moscow, became queen of France; and it is worth noting that after the death of her husband she had little regency and did not claim it. The laws change according to matters. It was the Count of Flanders, one of the king's vassals, who became regent. The widowed queen remarried a Count of Crepis. All this would have been singular today, and it was not so then. Neither Henry nor Philip I did anything memorable; but from their affairs and their vassals they conquered kingdoms.

Miss Iuliano commands to Torneto to take her and bring her back to him at his estate. There, she also stays clean as if she had never moved. The next day, she was brought back to the same place to see if anyone will sell her. But no one came, which he was very surprised: and thought that this must be some spirit that has taken her. From there, for some time, Master Arnaud writes to Miss Iuliano, which he found mounted on his horse, and says: Mr. Iuliano, I am very glad to know that this horse is yours. For sure, you are certain that it is good: I have tried it, and it has been about a year since I last saw her past the bridge of the Rosne, when she came alone there, and that a gardener wanted to take her. But in her way, as she was going about her life without knowing who she was with, I left her for a day or two without being able to know to whom she belonged. The third day, I stayed with her until Villeneufve, or rather, I say that a gentleman named François wanted to take her, and he had said that one should have seen them taken by a gardener on the way to Paris. The gentleman went afterward. And knowing this, I left him to go back for her: but I never reached him. For he was going far to reach his master. And while searching for him so much that I found myself in Lorraine, there, seeing that I did not hear any news from that gentleman, I kept him long. And at the end I returned to this city, or I caught up with him: and I found among my friends that he remembered well having seen her here: but he did not know to whom she belonged, except perhaps to some of you other men of the legation. Knowing this, I brought him to the Place du Palais so that whoever she was with might see him. And while I was going there from Nimes, or rather, I went back since two days, I was very sorry for her.

I have been employed to transcribe anything that is missing, a portion of what Messer Francesco di Nianto the Thuscan has written on how to read letters not apparent, and what script Zoroaster wrote in illegible characters. And Calpurnius Bassus from the books of illegible texts, but I do not see anything there, and I believe it is only water. Now let us look at it. When he saw it, they found inside it a scroll written in Hebrew, called Lamah Hazabthani, whose name was given to Epistemon, who was asking what it should say? A man named that the Hebrew language means, so why did I leave you, whom I secretly said to Panurge, and then he explained the matter. See you now. This is a diamond of flawed writing. Thusly is the explanation of what the lady intends. Diamond flawed for how I leave you? What explanation did Pantagruel understandably remember: that on his departure he had not spoken to God about the lady, and in distress: and they wished to return immediately to Paris to make peace with her. But Epistemon reduced him to a memoir of the depositions of Eneas with Dido, and the dictation by Heraclides Tarentinus: that the ship remaining at the anchor when necessity calls, it should cut its cord more than losing time in the sea. And that it must leave all thoughts for some moment to occur in the city of its birth, which is in danger. A few hours later, a wind called North-North-West arose, which they gave full strength and sailed the great sea, and in brief days passed by port at St. George, and by Medera, they set sail from the islands of Canaria.

Except for the only last volume which is a quadruped of bisulcus, whose war of King of Suecia has interrupted its continuation, and that the price of everything printed in Germany is 14 escus, but that the bookstores in Paris have not even one exemplary copy present at this time. On what I am waiting for your orders, I finish here, Mr. Pierre d'Antelme, 1631. Mr., it is too late to remain silent and I am very well pleased to have an opportunity to break it for you to tell me, please accept the protests of the continuation of my wishes for your service, that finally a small roll of a few new books has passed, among which there are enough curious ones and that I believe you will not be surprised by them. I have sent my bookshop to Aix to come and deliver them and to have means of making you participate in it. Among others we have had some small works by the poor Keplerus who are now in the hands of Mr. the Prévôt de La Valette at Aix, concerning the small eclipses of the sun which must arrive in these months of November and December, not by the interposition of the body of the moon, but from those of the planets Venus and Mercury which will also be as beautiful to observe as they are rare, arriving only once every few hundred years, through which excellent consequences can be drawn from their greatness and distance or separation from the earth. There is also a judgment by Keplerus on a book by an Jesuit from China concerning the astronomy of that country, which is said to be much more exact than ours, where there are beautiful things to see. If you could make a donation as far as possible, please accept these warmest wishes and give me some pleasant diversion.

text: The response of Count De Bussy to Madame De S. à Chaseu, dated September 1, 1675. In informing me that your letters are not worthy of my approval, madame, you write one that deserves greater approval, without counting your modesty. But to avoid offending her further, I will discuss another matter with you. What Monsieur the Prince of Monsieur De Turenne said as he passed through Châlons is proof of a very honest man and a man who feels well his merit. Monsieur De Montecuculi will be even more cautious with him than he was with Monsieur De Turenne. It is true that Chevalier De G was happy in the battle of Altenhein; and the pouch belonging to that of Consarbricq. I rejoice with you, and I hope to give you the same compliment for your son at the end of this campaign. You should tell me about the trial concerning it. I am so eager to hear from you that I would grant you a favorable audience when you speak only of intermediaries and stops. Letter 61. Response of Count De Bussy to Madame De S. à Chaseu, dated September 29, 1675. I received your letter yesterday, madame, which gave me the joy that your letters have accustomed me to giving you. Finally, you denied the point of passing; it will find what it seeks. Regarding seeking, this reminds me of the poor Chevalier De Rohan, who, on a very late evening in Fontainebleau, Madame D., who passed by in a gallery, asked her what she sought: nothing, said she. My faith, madame, is that he replied—he did not wish to have lost what you seek. Here is my little story, madame. You allowed me to make it as good, I use the freedom you granted me. I found your letter amusing at its last point, and I knew well enough that one must have a mind to find this as enjoyable as it is.

According to the comments of Caesar, there was another Gergovia in the land of the Gauls; but this second city is even less known than the previous one, although common opinion places it near Moulins in Bourbonnais. See the memoirs of the Academy of the Beautiful Letters, where you will find a dissertation by Mr. Lancelot on this subject. (D. J.) GERIS * GERIS, s. f. (Myth.) is the name of a deity that Hesychius believes to be the same as Cerès or Earth. GERMAIN GERMAIN, adj., is a quality attributed to certain parishes, and which has two different meanings. It is said to be called "sisters" and "Germains," to express those who are married on both sides; it is -to-say that they are conceived from the same father and mother. "Germain-Germains" are those who are separated by a degree greater than Germains-Germains. See Sisters & Cousins. (A) Germain in Laye, (Saint) is a small town on the island of France, with a royal house embellished by several of our kings. It is one of the most beautiful stays in France for its position, forest, and gardens. It is four leagues from Paris along the Seine. Long. 19. 40. lat. 48. 52. Marguerite of France, daughter of François I, was born at Saint-Germain-l'Évêque on June 5, 1523, and achieved immortality through her beauty, knowledge, and virtues. Her subjects called her the mother of the peoples. Henry II. was born in the same castle on May 31, 1518, and lived in Paris from July 10, 1559, after a lance shot that he received in a tournament, persecuted the Calvinists in his kingdom, allied with the Swiss, who struggled to do so, and was soon opposed by the wills of the duchess of Valentinois, who became his mistress of his heart and mind, although she was forty-seven years old.
